column1: A New Range of 3D Models Now available from Medstore in full detail
column6:
Product information "Abdomen with bilateral Hernias"
\nThis 3D model represents one of the largest and most complex in the series, consisting of a partial torso from the diaphragm to the proximal thigh with a complete abdominal cavity preserving varying levels of dissection. This 3D model also records the rare, simultaneous occurrence of indirect and direct inguinal hernias allowing for a consideration of the anatomical underpinnings for both conditions. Given the scale of the dissection this 3D model description is divided into discrete parts based on views and regions.
\n
\nThe diaphragm
\nOn the superior aspect of the model the diaphragm is preserved, and while slightly distorted due to removal of the thoracic ribs through dissection, both domes and costodiaphragmatic recesses can be appreciated. The fibrous pericardium is present on the superior surface of the central tendon, with the terminal part of the inferior vena cava visible in the caval foramen. Just lateral to caval foramen is the oesophagus within the oesophageal hiatus, and then the descending thoracic aorta approaching the aortic hiatus just ventral to the thoracic vertebrae.
\n
\nThe epigastric and hypochondriac regions
\nWithin the abdomen, the anterior abdominal wall, greater omentum, and much of the gastrointestinal tract has been removed alongside the parietal peritoneum over the posterior abdominal wall to expose retroperitoneal organs and structures. In the superior abdomen, the terminal portion of the oesophagus has been retained and can be seen entering the cavity just lateral to the left lobe of the liver. The removal of the stomach has exposed the extent of the pancreas from the head (positioned within the arc of the duodenum) to the tail extending to the capsule of the spleen preserved in the left hypochondrium. Superior to the pancreas, the splenic artery and common hepatic arteries can just be observed spanning across the narrow space between the pancreas, diaphragm and liver. The splenic follows its archetypical ‘tortuous route’ towards the spleen, and strongly divides prior to reaching the hilum (and adjacent to the splenic vein). The common hepatic can be seen dividing into the gastroduodenal (visible again as a cut vessel just inferior to the duodenum) and giving off the right gastric artery; these vessels lie superficial relative to the hepatic portal vein. The superior mesenteric artery and vein can be seen passing anteriorly near the head of the pancreas and horizontal part of the duodenum, and the retained ileocolic artery can be traced to the caecum of the large intestine in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen. The inferior mesenteric vein can be, in part, appreciated arising from the retained superior rectal vein ascending from the undissected true pelvis and spanning across the superficial aspect of the descending thoracic aorta.
\n
\nInferior to the liver the gallbladder can be viewed just between the right and left anatomical lobes. On the left, the passage of the renal artery and vein can be seen just deep to the pancreas, and the ureters can be observed descending from the partially exposed kidney across the superficial surface of the exposed psoas major and minor muscles.
\n
\nThe umbilical and lumbar regions
\nMost of the organs occupying the umbilical and lumbar regions of the abdomen have been removed in order to expose structures in the posterior abdominal wall. In the midline, the descending abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava dominate the region, with the testicular arteries and veins isolated and traceable towards the inguinal regions. Two right lumbar arteries are visible arising from the aorta, and despite removal of the mesenteries and most of the colon the inferior mesenteric artery can be seen giving rise to the left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries. On the right side of the specimen inferior to the kidney, the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioingual nerves are exposed alongside the circumflex iliac artery.
\n

Sugar solutions are optically active, in other words they rotate the plane of polarisation of any linearly polarised light that is passed through them. The direction of rotation depends on the molecular properties of the sugar. Thus, solutions of glucose and saccharose (sucrose) rotate the plane of polarisation to the right (clockwise), whereas fructose solutions rotate it to the left (counter-clockwise), as found when the angle of rotation is measured with a polarimeter. The experiment also includes measuring the angle of rotation to study the behaviour of a saccharose solution when hydrochloric acid is added. This causes a gradual reversal (“inversion”) of the direction of rotation from clockwise to counter-clockwise, as the double-ring structure of the saccharose molecule is split into two, giving an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose. The angle of rotation of the mixture is the sum of the angles of rotation of the dextro-rotatory glucose and the more strongly laevo-rotatory fructose.

column1: A Paper of Advantages of the Sonksen Logmar test System over alternative Systems
column6:
PURPOSE To develop a standardized logMAR test of visual acuity for young children and establish 
\ntestability and reliability. 
\nMETHODS Two thousand nine hundred ninety-one children, aged 2 to 8 years 6 months, from a 
\npopulation sample of 4671 were recruited from schools and preschool facilities and tested. 
\nAbility to name or match letters, accept occlusion, and achieve binocular single and 
\nbinocular and monocular measures of linear visual acuity were recorded. Inter- and 
\nintratester reliability was assessed for a random selection of 215 children. 
\nRESULTS Two thousand nine hundred seventy-four (99.4%) matched or named letters, 2966 (99%) 
\nachieved binocular single, 2940 (98%) achieved binocular linear, and 2807 (94%) achieved 
\nmonocular linear (for both eyes) measures. Binocular linear measures were achieved in 
\n50% aged less than 3 years, 80% aged 3 to 3½, 92% aged 3½ to 4, and 99% aged 4 years 
\nand over. Binocular linear measures were achieved in 86% of 2- to 3-year-olds and 96% 
\nof 3- to 3½-year-olds who matched or named letters; monocular linear measures were 
\nachieved in 86 and 95%, respectively, of these age groups who then accepted occlusion. 
\nThe median time for completion of the test ( binocular and monocular) was 3 minutes 55 
\nseconds. The 95% limits of agreement for the same observer and for different observers 
\nwere 0.13 and -0.19, +0.15 for binocular linear and -0.16, +0.15, and -0.17, +0.13 
\nfor monocular linear measures, respectively. 
\nCONCLUSIONS The Sonksen logMAR Test provides reliable binocular and monocular measures of linear 
\nvisual acuity in a high proportion of children from the age of 2.5 years. ( J
\n
\n
\nT 
\nesting the visual acuity of young children in accord 
\nwith adult standards has posed problems to test 
\ndesigners over several decades. 
\n1-4 
\nMany designers 
\nhave introduced stimulus modiﬁcations in attempts to sim- 
\nplify the developmental content, for example, using sym- 
\nbols instead of letters. 
\n5,6,7 
\nThe Sonksen Silver Acuity System successfully ad- 
\ndressed many of the developmental problems of letter- 
\nbased tests for young children, while adhering strictly to 
\nthe speciﬁcations of the Snellen standard, and was the ﬁrst 
\nto introduce single-line test displays in a ﬂip-over book- 
\nlet. 
\n8 
\nIn 1995 our group demonstrated high testability even 
\nof the youngest children for this test and maturation in 
\nvisual acuity between 2 years 6 months and 9 years. 
\n9,10 
\nThe Consilium of Ophthalmologists decided that the 
\nlogMAR scaling devised by Bailey and Lovie in 1976 
\nhad advantages over Snellen scaling and is now the 
\naccepted gold standard. 
\n11-14 
\nWhen we decided to design 
\nthe Sonksen logMAR test, existing logMAR tests for 
\nchildren were published without norms: in some the 
\nspacing between optotypes was less than that speciﬁed 
\nfor adult tests, such as the ETDRS. 
\n15-18 
\nSuch factors 
\ncompromise the interpretation of measurement in terms 
\nof the adult standard and the accuracy of monitoring 
\nchanges in visual acuity due to treatment or progress of 
\ndisease from childhood into early adult life. A standard 
\nlogMAR test system together with testability, reliability, 
\nand norms was therefore needed for preschool and 
\nyoung school-age children. 
\nIn this article we present the ﬁrst two stages in the 
\ndevelopment of the Sonksen logMAR Test: (1) test 
\ndesign and standardized protocol and (2) testability and 
\nreliability. We present the third stage—the develop- 
\nment of age norms—in the companion article. 
\n19 
\nThe 
\nnew test has logMAR scaling, uses international chart 
\ndesign standard letter optotypes with constant contour 
\ninteraction, and uses a standard test protocol that in-
\n
\ncludes features aimed at enhancing testability of the 
\nyoungest age groups. 
\nMaterials and Methods 
\nEthical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committees of 
\nCambridge District ( UK) and the Institute of Child Health 
\nLondon. Data collection was organized and collated by the re- 
\nsearch orthoptist and administrator. Five other community or- 
\nthoptists assisted the research orthoptist with vision testing after 
\ninstruction in the standard test protocol (see e-Supplement 1, 
\navailable at jaapos.org); this ensured uniformity of test adminis- 
\ntration throughout the study. 
\nDesign of the Sonksen logMAR Test 
\nDevelopmental Features. In designing the Sonksen Sil- 
\nver Acuity System and the Sonksen logMAR Test, we adhered to 
\nfundamental developmental principals of test design: when 
\nadapting test design to suit an age or disability group, one 
\nmodiﬁes/simpliﬁes the instructions and response task to suit the 
\ngroup while maintaining the fabric/standard of the test content. 
\nThe developmental features of the Sonksen logMAR Test and of 
\nthe test protocol are similar to those of the Sonksen Silver Acuity 
\nSystem, 
\n8 
\nwith a training booklet, keycard, one single-letter, and 
\ntwo linear ﬂip-over test booklets, pointer, and occlusion specta- 
\ncles. Each page of the linear test booklets presents a single line of 
\nfour letters with crowding bars. The letters O, X, H, T, U, and 
\nV were selected as these are the easiest for young children to 
\nmatch. 
\n2 
\nA test distance of 3 m was chosen as this enhances 
\nrapport and helps maintain the attention of the youngest children 
\nwithout affecting contour interaction or decreasing sensitivity or 
\ndetection rate of myopia. 
\n20,21 
\nA ﬂip-over booklet of crowded 
\nsingle letters was used to facilitate choosing a suitable starting 
\nlevel in the linear booklet as young children are likely to tire and 
\ngive erratic responses if asked to identify all the test letters on an 
\neye chart. 
\nTest Speciﬁcations. The speciﬁcations recommended by 
\nthe Consilium of Ophthalmologists and others were closely ad- 
\nhered to in the test design. 
\n11,12,18,22 
\nOptotypes and the spacing 
\nbetween them conform to ETDRS speciﬁcations, that is, letters 
\nare 5 minutes of arc square, without serifs, and with stroke width 
\nequivalent to 1 minute of arc at every level. Spacing between 
\noptotypes is equal to one letter width. Figure 1 illustrates a linear 
\ntest display. (For full design details, see e-Supplement 1 and the 
\nFigure 1 legend.) 
\nTest Protocol. Younger children are seated at a low table 
\nand trained in letter matching using the training booklet and 
\nkeycard if unable to name letters. Children are then asked to 
\nidentify each of the letters in the booklet of single-letter displays 
\npresented at 3 m starting with the 0.7 letter until a letter is not 
\nseen correctly. The smallest letter seen is recorded as the child’s 
\nbinocular visual acuity for singles. The test display two logMAR 
\nlevels above the singles failure in the ﬁrst linear test booklet is 
\nthen presented. If a child is unable to see some of the letters at 
\nthe starting level, the tester should present the preceding larger 
\ndisplays until a full line is identiﬁed; the child is then shown each 
\nletter in turn until three consecutive letters are failed. Every 
\nletter correctly identiﬁed after the last whole line achieved con- 
\ntributes to the score. 
\n23 
\nOcclusion spectacles are then introduced 
\nand monocular acuity is ascertained using the second booklet of 
\nlinear displays for the right eye and the ﬁrst booklet for the left 
\neye. The time taken for each phase of testing was recorded. (For 
\nfuller details, see e-Supplement 1.) 
\nStudy Design. The design of the study was cross-sectional 
\nand population based. 
\nRecruitment. Children aged 2 years to 8 years 8 months 
\nwere recruited through Cambridge ( UK) city, state, and private 
\nsector schools, nurseries, and playgroups. No visual defect or 
\nimpairment criteria were applied. Parents/guardians who gave 
\nconsent provided information on demographics and prior vision 
\ntreatment via a questionnaire. Class listings were used to ascer- 
\ntain the total population from which the responders were drawn 
\nand to check demographic data, including gender and postal 
\ncode. Ethnicity was recorded at the time of testing. Socioeco- 
\nnomic status was based on the Townsend Index, which provides 
\na material measure of deprivation and disadvantage based on data 
\nfrom the 2001 UK population census. Higher Townsend index 
\nscores are associated with higher deprivation and disadvantage. 
\n24 
\nTesting. Ability to match or name letters, to accept oc- 
\nclusion, and to achieve the four measures of visual acuity— 
\nbinocular singles, binocular linear, and monocular linear 
\n(right eye then left eye)—were recorded together with the 
\nmeasures achieved. Spectacles, if worn (4% of children tested), 
\nwere removed during testing. Patients who failed to meet 
\npredeﬁned visual acuity criteria were referred for ophthalmo- 
\nlogic evaluation. 
\nReliability. A random selection of 215 children were re- 
\ntested within 11 days, 103 by the same orthoptist, to ascertain the 
\nlevel of inter- and intratester reliability. These children came 
\nfrom across the test sites to ensure a distribution of ages in line
\n
\n
\n
\nThe number of children wearing glasses or already re- 
\nceiving ophthalmic treatment was 195/3014 (6.5%), which 
\nis similar to the number of expected ocular or vision 
\ndefects requiring treatment or follow-up in the general 
\npreschool population. 
\n27-29 
\nFor those who consented, there was no difference in the 
\npresence of a known eye/vision problem or English as ﬁrst 
\nlanguage between those tested and those who were absent 
\nor “unwilling” to be tested on the day. 
\nTestability 
\nTable 1 presents testability with 95% conﬁdence intervals 
\n(CI) for each age group and the factors that inﬂuence 
\nability to complete the “test”—achieving binocular and 
\nmonocular linear visual acuity measures for both right and 
\nleft eyes. Of the total 2991 children tested, 2807 (94%) 
\ncompleted the test. Almost all (2236/2270 [99%]) children 
\naged 4 years and older completed the test; 50% of children 
\nunder 3 years old, 80% of 3- to 3½-year-olds, and 92% of 
\n3½- to 4-year-olds did so. 
\nDevelopmental factors (ability to letter match and to ac- 
\ncept occlusion) inﬂuenced the ability of children less than 4 
\nyears old to complete the test. Letter matching was achieved 
\nin 94 to 100% of children from 2½ years. Of those able to 
\nletter match, 87% (95% CI, 80-92) of children under 3 years 
\nold, 96% (95% CI, 93-99) of 3 to 3½-year-olds achieved a 
\nbinocular linear visual acuity measure. Only 7 of the 2630 
\n(0.3%) children aged 3½ and older who were able to letter 
\nmatch did not complete the binocular linear test. 
\nAcceptance of occlusion was lowest in children under 
\n3½ years. Of those who had achieved a binocular measure, 
\n73% (95% CI, 65-81) of under 3 years old, 91% (95% CI, 
\n87-95) of 3- to 3½-year-olds, and 95% (95% CI, 92-97) of 
\n3½- to 4-year-olds accepted occlusion. Subsequently 
\n74/86 (86-95% CI, 79-93) of under 3-year-olds and 171/ 
\n181 (94.5-95% CI, 91-98) of 3- to 3½-year-olds who had 
\naccepted occlusion achieved monocular measures. From 
\nthe age of 3½ years, more than 99% of those accepting 
\nocclusion completed the test. 
\nThe median administration time, the range, and 
\ninterquartile range by age group is given in Figure 3. In 
\nchildren unable to name letters, time taken included train- 
\ning to letter match. The median time for completion of a 
\nbinocular single and linear measures was 2 minutes, 1 
\nsecond and for completion of both binocular and monoc- 
\nular testing was 3 minutes, 55 seconds. Even in children 
\nyounger than 3 years, the median time to complete both 
\nbinocular and monocular tasks was 6 minutes with a min- 
\nimum of 3 minutes, 7 seconds. 
\nReliability 
\nThe Bland-Altman plots of within (A) and between (B) 
\northoptist reliability are shown in Figure 4 for binocular 
\nlinear measures and Figure 5 for monocular linear mea- 
\nsures— only right eyes were retested. For all measures 
\nthere was good agreement on average between repeat tests 
\nfor both the same and different observers. The limits of 
\nagreement show the range within which 95% of differ- 
\nences are expected to lie. The average difference and limits 
\nof agreement are shown on the plots together with 95% 
\nconﬁdence intervals. The conﬁdence intervals show the 
\nprecision of the mean and limit estimates. 
\nFor the same observer, the mean difference between 
\nrepeat test scores for binocular linear visual acuity was 
\n0.0024 logMAR (95% CI, -0.010-0.015) and the 95% 
\nlimits of agreement were 0.13 logMAR (5.2 letters). 
\nFor different observers the mean difference was -0.016 
\n(95% CI, -0.032-0) and the 95% limits of agreement 
\nwere -0.19, +0.15 logMAR (-7.6, +6 letters). For the 
\nsame observer the mean difference between repeat test 
\nscores for monocular linear visual acuity was -0.0082 
\n(95% CI, -0.024-0.007) and the 95% limits of agreement 
\nwere -0.16, +0.15 logMAR (-6.4, +6 letters). For dif- 
\nferent observers, the mean difference was -0.0188 (95% 
\nCI, -0.034-0.004) and the 95% limits of agreement were 
\n-0.17, +0.13 logMAR (-6.8-5.2 letters). 
\nThere were no signiﬁcant trends in differences with 
\naverage visual acuity level for single and linear binocular 
\nand linear monocular measures ( p = 0.352, 0.106, and 
\n0.269, respectively). 
\nRegression analysis was used to determine whether the 
\ndifferences in repeat measurements of single and linear 
\nbinocular and linear monocular visual acuity varied ac- 
\ncording to whether the tested differed between repeats, 
\nhow long there was between repeats, the age of the child, 
\nand/or their gender. The results for each of the four 
\nfactors are shown separately in Table 2. The p-values show 
\n
\nto symbols and are presented in single lines with constant 
\ncontour interaction. Other tests developed for pediatric 
\npopulations (eg, Kay and Lea symbol charts) use nonstand- 
\nard picture stimuli 
\n1,30 
\nor reduced spacing (increasing con- 
\ntour interaction) of letters (eg, the Keeler logMAR Test) 
\n7 
\ncompared with the adult standard. These variations make 
\naccurate comparisons difﬁcult as the child matures and 
\nadult tests are used. 
\nThis large population-based study of children aged 2 to 
\n8 years 8 months using the Sonksen logMAR Test shows 
\nhigh testability for both binocular and monocular testing 
\neven in children aged 2½ to 3 years. Sonksen introduced 
\nfeatures into the design of the Sonksen Silver Acuity Sys- 
\ntem to reduce the developmental complexity of the test 
\ntask and proposed a test protocol that improved testability 
\nin the youngest children. 
\n8 
\nWe incorporated similar devel- 
\nopmental features and standard test protocol into the 
\nSonksen logMAR Test and again found high levels of 
\nachievement for monocular measures—51% of 2½- to 
\n3-year-olds, 80% of 3- to 3½-year-olds, and 92% of 3½- 
\nto 4-year-olds. The important developmental features of 
\nthe protocol are: (1) sitting the child at a nursery table and 
\nchair, (2) using the techniques described to train matching 
\nand level ﬁnding, and (3) taking a full binocular linear 
\nvisual acuity measure before attempting occlusion. 
\n8,9 
\nAd- 
\nministration time for the test is very acceptable for a 
\nscreening or diagnostic program and similar to that re- 
\nported by others. 
\n9,31,32 
\nMost studies have either not included 
\n33 
\nor have reported 
\npoorer testability than found in this study in under 3½- 
\nyear-olds. 
\n34-38 
\nGroups who have looked at testability in 
\n3-year-olds often fail to report separately on 3- to 3½- 
\nyear-olds and 3½- to 4-year-olds. In this study testability 
\nwas considerably better in the older group, suggesting that 
\ntestability is likely to be falsely high in a group of 3-year- 
\nolds if the distribution is weighted in favor of the older age 
\nbracket. 
\nThe rationale for starting with a monocular test even in 
\nyoung children has been the clinical priority to identify 
\namblyopia. Our experience and the ﬁndings of our current 
\nand previous studies suggests that completing binocular 
\ntesting ﬁrst familiarizes a child with the test procedure 
\nbefore adding the additional demands of occlusion and 
\nthereby increases success with monocular testing. 
\n9 
\nIn this 
\nstudy testability is higher in 2- to 5-year-olds than in 
\nrecent studies by others using protocols that start, as rec- 
\nommended by the Task Force 
\n12 
\nwith instruction in letter 
\nmatching ( binocular pretesting) at 1 or 3 m. 
\n30,31,36 
\nThe 
\nclinical value of full binocular testing is highlighted by the 
\nﬁndings of two large epidemiologic surveys of visual acuity 
\nin childhood and two evaluation studies, which show that 
\nlittle reliability in detection of uniocular problems is 
\nlost in patients without strabismus, by achieving a bin- 
\nocular measure only. 
\n27-29,39 
\nOn the basis of the above 
\nevidence and as developmental experts with a major 
\ninterest in vision, we advocate that a full binocular 
\nmeasure is undertaken before attempting occlusion or 
\nmonocular testing in under 5-year-olds. 
\nThe 95% limits of agreement of logMAR scores for the 
\nSonksen logMAR Test found in this study for monocular 
\nvisual acuity for the same (-0.16, 0.15) and different 
\nobserver (-0.17, 0.13) was in keeping with that previously 
\nreported for logMAR-based tests in adult subjects and in 
\nolder children (5 to 9 years) (+0.14, -0.14 to +0.2, -0.2), 
\ndespite the inclusion of young children in this co- 
\nhort. 
\n12,40-42 
\nA clinically relevant change in visual acuity 
\nwould from these results have to fall outside the 95% 
\nlimits of agreement, that is, for two measures made by the 
\nsame observer, a clinically relevant difference would be 
\nthat deemed to be outside the expected differences that 
\nwould be observed between repeats anyway: more than ﬁve 
\nletters for binocular visual acuity and more than seven 
\nletters for monocular visual acuity. 
\nDifferences in repeat measures were not signiﬁcantly 
\ninﬂuenced by any of the factors examined. The most 
\nmarginal results were for age; however, the point estimates 
\nshow that any differences are small. For example, the 
\nestimated change with age for single binocular repeats is 
\nnegative, indicating better agreement for older children as 
\nwould be expected, yet the fall is only estimated to be 
\n0.00098 per year and even over the entire age range in- 
\nvestigated (2-9 years) this is an estimated change of less 
\nthan 0.007 (less than one letter). On the basis of these 
\nresults, it is reasonable to infer that clinically important 
\ndifferences did not occur. Although the sample sizes are 
\nnot large for some subgroups, the coefﬁcients and conﬁ- 
\n
\n
\ndence intervals suggest that clinically important differ- 
\nences were not missed due to a lack of power. 
\nThe strengths of this study are the adherence to inter- 
\nnational test design standards, an acceptable response rate 
\n(70%) with consent only withheld actively in 77 (1.6%), 
\nand the size and representativeness in terms of ethnicity 
\nand socioeconomic status of the population-based cohort 
\nto that of the UK. 
\nLimitations include lack of demographic data concern- 
\ning nonresponders as demographic details were only col- 
\nlected with the returned consent. The potential bias of 
\nparents of children with visual difﬁculties being less or 
\nmore likely to respond is unlikely given the prevalence of 
\ndefects found in the population tested. 
\nConclusions 
\nThis article presents the ﬁrst two stages in development of 
\nthe Sonksen logMAR Test, a new test for children that 
\naccords with the adult standard and with a standard test 
\nprotocol. Levels of testability are higher and reliability 
\ndata are comparable to other tests. Stage 3, the derivation 
\nof age norms, is presented in the companion article.

\nProduct information "Spleen and pancreas"
\nThis 3D model preserves the deep foregut organs: the descending, horizontal and ascending duodenum, the pancreas, and the spleen. A small window in the duodenum has been opened to allow for a view of the plicae circularis within this proximal part of the small intestine (and contrasts the strong rugae development seen in the stomach; see AW 42). The head of the pancreas is preserved in its normal position within the curvature of the duodenum, and a distinct uncus can be observed at the distal margin and adjacent to the exiting of the superior mesenteric artery (already divided into its numerous named branches). Along the superior margin of the body of the pancreas, the celiac trunk has been sectioned from the descending abdominal aorta. The complete splenic artery can be observed on its tortuous route from origin to the spleen, as well as the bases of the left gastric artery and common hepatic artery. Immediately adjacent to the celiac trunk is a small part of the splenic vein, which emerges from within the capsule of the pancreas, and is in part visible in along its route near the splenic artery. A small portion of the superior mesenteric vein adheres to the posterior aspect of the pancreas, representing the course of the vessel before it would normally join the splenic and form the hepatic portal vein. \nProduct information "Liver with vessels and gallbladder"
\nThe size and shape of this specimen varies somewhat from a typical liver. It is less wedge-shaped and longer in the superoinferior dimension (on the posterior view this would translate to a greater vertical height). Normally, a liver is less than 16cm in the midclavicular line.1 This specimen measures approximately 18cm in the midclavicular line, suggesting some degree of hepatomegaly. However, it is worth mentioning that some measurement distortion may have occurred based on the fixing and curation of the specimen – and it must be noted that the accuracy of estimating liver size using a single parameter is limited. Liver measurements diagnostic of hepatomegaly vary depending on normal anatomical variation in liver size and morphology, the method of measurement, and patient features such as sex and BMI.
\nAn alternative explanation could be normal anatomical variation. However, this specimen does not fit the description of the most common anatomical variations confused with hepatomegaly – Riedel’s lobe (a downward projection of the right lobe), ‘beaver tail’ liver (an elongated left lobe), or a papillary process projecting from the caudate lobe.

\nProduct information "Female pelvis deep dissection"
\nThis 3D model presents a deep dissection and isolation of the pelvis from surrounding regions, particularly demonstrating visceral and neurovascular structures relative to deep ligaments and osseous features.
\nWithin the false pelvis, the sigmoid colon descends on the left side of the specimen to the rectum, passing superficially across the pelvic brim and the passage of the common and external iliac artery and vein. Adjacent to the sigmoid colon are parts of the sigmoid arteries and superior rectal artery, resting superficial to the common iliac vessels and near the descending ureter. Anterior in the true pelvis is the collapsed urinary bladder, and between the bladder and rectum rests the uterus. The organ is partially covered in the broad ligament, with both the suspensory ligament of the ovary and round ligament have been separated and pulled away from the peritoneum on both sides to expose surrounding blood vessels. While the ovarian ligaments, round ligaments, uterine tubes and ovaries are trapped within the peritoneal fold of the broad ligament, the reduction in ovary size (common with advanced age) has rendered these indistinguishable in the model.
\n
\nLateral to these organs, branches of the internal iliac artery can be identified – as well as a retained median sacral artery in the midline between the two common iliac arteries. On the left side only the uterine artery can be seen laterally. On the right side, the obturator, superior vesical, and uterine arteries can be observed. In addition, the origins of the inferior epigastric artery and vein can be seen arising from the external iliac vessels just prior to exiting the inferior abdominal cavity.
\nOn the right side of the preserved pelvis, the entire femur and thigh musculature has been removed to demonstrate the obturator membrane, the articular cartilage of the acetabulum and the transverse ligament of the acetabulum. Posteriorly the entire gluteal region has been dissected to expose the superior gluteal foramen and the origin of the superior gluteal artery. The sacrotuberous ligament has been removed to demonstrate the sacrospinous ligament, with some branches of the inferior rectal artery retained within the exposed ischoanal fossa.
\nOn the left side of the preserved pelvis the sciatic nerve has been maintained within the greater sciatic foramen, as has the sacrotuberous ligament. The ischioanal fossa mirrors that of the right side, where branches of the inferior rectal artery have been retained relative to the fibres of the pelvic diaphragm, and the integration of the external anal sphincter on the projecting external rectal surface.

Product information "Canine Thoracic Cavity"
\nThis specimen presents a right-side dissection of the thoracic cavity (Cavitas thoracis) of an adult dog. Following removal of the right thoracic wall, including the ribs (costae), the right lung (pulmo dexter) has been excised, leaving the pulmonary vessels (vasa pulmonalia) in situ in relation to the heart (cor). In the cranial mediastinum (mediastinum craniale), the veins forming the cranial vena cava (vena cava cranialis) are identifiable, along with the course of branches from the right subclavian artery (arteria subclavia dextra). Also visible in this region are the thoracic portion of the longus colli muscle (musculus longus colli), the thoracic trachea (trachea thoracica), and the thoracic esophagus (esophagus thoracicus).
\n

In the middle mediastinum (mediastinum medium), the heart (cor), partially covered by the fibrous pericardium (pericardium fibrosum), is visible. At its base (basis cordis), the pulmonary vessels and the principal bronchi (bronchi principales) — formed by the division of the trachea — can be observed.
\n
\nThe caudal mediastinum (mediastinum caudale) reveals the course of the caudal vena cava (vena cava caudalis) and the right phrenic nerve (nervus phrenicus dexter), adjacent to the caudal mediastinal recess (recessus mediastini caudalis), which is defined by the fold of the caudal vena cava (plica venae cavae). The dorsal aspect is occupied by the esophagus (esophagus), along which travel the dorsal and ventral vagal trunks (truncus vagalis dorsalis et ventralis), as well as the thoracic aorta (aorta thoracica), the right azygos vein (vena azygos dextra), and the sympathetic trunk (truncus sympathicus).

Additionally, the extensor musculature of the cervical and thoracic spine (musculi extensores columnae vertebralis cervicalis et thoracicae), the intercostal muscles (musculi intercostales), and the brachial plexus (plexus brachialis) are retained.

\nProduct information "Male hemipelvis and thigh"
\nThis 3D model preserves a right male pelvis sectioned just superior to the L5 vertebra and sectioned at the midsagittal plane, with the thigh preserved to near the midshaft of the femur. This specimen compliments our LW 91 female hemipelvic specimen and thigh.
\n
\nThe common iliac artery is preserved with several key branches visible, particularly the distribution of the internal iliac within the true pelvis. Several major vessels including the obturator artery and the partially obliterated umbilical artery passes towards the anterior abdominal wall (to form the medial umbilical ligament) and gives off the superior vesicle artery; while the roots of the iliolumbar, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal and internal pudendal artery are visible lateral to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends superficial to these vessels to approach the urinary bladder which is covered with peritoneum in this model. The ductus deferens is exposed from the entry into the space via the deep inguinal ring and passing posteriorly (though sectioned from its normal insertion pathway and resting on the internal iliac artery). Adjacent to the ureter and on the superficial surface of the psoas major muscle is an enlarged iliac lymph node and part of the lymphatic vasculature ascending along the external iliac artery. The majority of the pelvis has been left undissected, allowing for an appreciation of the rectovesicular pouch and the exposed superior rectal artery and vein approaching the preserved portion of rectum. In cross section, the rectum, seminal vesicle and prostate are visible (the section plane preserves parts of both the prostatic urethra and ejaculatory duct).
\n
\nIn the anterior thigh the borders and contents of the femoral triangle are well-preserved, with partial coverage by the flap of the anterior abdominal wall. Posteriorly the skin over the gluteal region and the gluteus maximus muscle have been removed as sequential windows to expose the gluteus medius and minimum muscles, the piriformis, the obturator internus with gemelli muscles, and the quadratus femoris muscle. The superior and inferior gluteal arteries are maintained superior and inferior to the piriformis, respectively; with the sciatic nerve exiting inferior to piriformis before passing deep to the retained portion of the gluteus maximus.

You can use the TN GOLD 80 to determine whether gold or silver bars and coins are genuine or whether they contain a core of a different material
\nThe instrument measures the thickness of gold bars and gold coins using ultrasound
\nProcess: Ultrasound waves are directed onto the test object using a sensor. The waves penetrate the test object, are then reflected from a surface opposite the object and then picked up again by the sensor. The measurement determined by this process will be compared with the material thickness as measured by a traditional calliper gauge. On the basis of the measurement given, false cores (Figure: grey) for example, those made of tungsten, lead, etc. can be easily identified, as the ultrasound reacts differently, compared with pure gold
\nSelectable measuring units: mm inch
\nSAUTER SSG software (included) can be used to calculate the sound velocity for various precious metal alloys. This makes it possible to determine whether coins or ingots contain false cores or whether they consist of one and the same material. Compatible with the following operating systems: Windows® 7/8/10
\nKnown additions in tested gold items – e.g. copper or silver – are compensated by the software

\nProduct information "Cubital Fossa"
\nThis 3D printed cubital fossa presents a superficial dissection of the right distal arm and proximal forearm.
\nThe skin and superficial fascia have been removed anteriorly, medially, and laterally to reveal the superficial veins—basilic, cephalic, and median cubital—as well as the cutaneous nerves (medial, lateral, and posterior antebrachial).
\n
\nDeep Fascia and Connective Tissue
\nThe deep fascia underlying the superficial structures has largely been removed, but the antebrachial fascia is retained medially to demonstrate the merging of connective tissue fibers with the tendon of the biceps brachii through the bicipital aponeurosis. Medially, the ulnar artery is visible entering the cubital tunnel proximal to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Anteriorly, the median nerve, brachial artery, and accompanying veins run parallel to the biceps brachii. On the lateral aspect, the cephalic vein rests on the brachioradialis muscle, while the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve lies on the common origin of the forearm extensors, just anterior to the exposed origin of the triceps brachii.
\n
\nCross-Sectional Anatomy
\nThe proximal cross-section displays the anterior and posterior arm compartment muscles (biceps brachii, brachialis, triceps brachii), neurovascular bundles (median, ulnar, and radial nerves; brachial artery and veins), and superficial veins (basilic and cephalic) at the midshaft of the humerus.
\n
\nThe distal cross-section reveals the anterior and posterior forearm compartment muscles separated by the interosseous membrane, along with superficial and deep neurovascular bundles (radial artery, vein, and superficial branch of the radial nerve; ulnar artery, vein, and nerve; median nerve; anterior and posterior interosseous arteries, veins, and nerves) and the distal continuations of the superficial veins and cutaneous nerves.

Thigh & Femoral Triangle

Gluteal Region
A window in gluteus maximus exposes piriformis, superior and inferior gluteal vessels, sciatic nerve, internal pudendal vessels, obturator internus, gemelli muscles, and proximal hamstrings, illustrating deep gluteal anatomy.
